Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself

vignette: When Naledi was held in the windowless detention room, her captors used isolation and fire as tools of control, stripping away all sound until the absence of noise became as heavy as the restraints, while forcing her to watch men with charred flesh and open wounds as burning scrap piled against the walls. That specific history explains why the sudden quiet of an underground rail tunnel, the sight of a bloodied cut on a commuter's hand, and the faint whiff of wildfire smoke near the freight yard do not merely startle her-they actively pull the old, disjointed pictures of the basement back into her mind. Because these sensory cues instantly summon the uncoordinated fragments, the memories continuously trigger each other, so that ordinary quiet or a stranger's wound instantly register as active threat reminders that cannot be ignored. Her mind's refusal to stitch these fragments into a timeline dictates how she copes. When the visual memories become too vivid, she immediately defaults to worst-case rehearsal, mentally scripting disaster scenarios to manage the disorientation, which in turn drives her to light a cigarette and constantly scan her own arms for fresh marks. Because the sudden quiet, the sight of injuries, and the smell of smoke trigger immediate distress, she quickly defaults to those same maladaptive routines, using body monitoring and smoking to dampen the panic before the images surge forward. The way her mind clings to those fragmented pictures then dictates how she survives the day. Because the memories persist as sharp, unlinked flashes rather than a settled story, she constantly scans the cab for sudden movements, interpreting any shift as imminent danger. Her hyperarousal and the coping habits quickly feed one another. Because she cannot relax, even in her locked apartment, the chronic physical tension keeps her intrusion monitoring active, which directly fuels her compulsive body checking and the habit of smoking to ground the panic. Yet the coping itself keeps the trauma alive. Her relentless habit of mentally rehearsing disasters fractures her recall further, locking her in disjointed flashes instead of allowing the past to organize, while the chronic threat monitoring keeps her nervous system hyper-alert, which actively sustains the intrusive images and prevents them from fading. The exhaustion from incessant scanning and smoking drains her capacity to decompress, ensuring her threat response never truly powers down. Over the months, this cycle carved itself into her work as a train conductor. She began arriving hours early to the depot, not to review schedules, but to sit in the idling cab and meticulously map every possible route out, her fingers constantly tracing her ribs for tenderness. Her husband noticed the distance first. She stopped answering his calls when the train passed through the mountain tunnels, fearing that the sudden drop in ambient noise would drop her back into the room. The constant scanning for smoke or movement left her voice thin and her shoulders rigid, turning shared dinners into silent vigils. What finally brought her to the clinic was the morning she stood at the controls of a loaded passenger train, unable to distinguish whether the heat she felt was from the engine or from the phantom burn of the scrapyard floor. She wants to feel the tracks beneath her without bracing for collapse, and she is most afraid that her mind will never let her believe she is truly out of the room.
